title: Busch's Barber Shop
author: Michael Eidem (Kellogg 2020); edited by Rohan Maini (Kellogg 2020)
case_type_source_label: Y04 Market entry; Y06 Opportunity assessment
fit_question: Tell me something about yourself that is not on your resume.
prompt: Your friend, a current MBA student, has his heart set on starting a barbershop in Evanston after graduation. There are plenty of barbershops and salons near the Northwestern campus, but your eager friend argues they are either (A) vastly overpriced or (B) cheap, but really low quality. He wants your help coming up with a plan.

clarifying_info.answer: For this analysis, your friend wants to focus solely on a target market of the male population of Evanston.
Highly competitive, segmented into two distinct groups (high price & low price). Friend believes there is a profitable space in between these two segments.
Growing at GDP over the past five years.

No specific experience in the cosmetology area; has enough savings to fund initial upfront costs and early ongoing costs. Profitability is the main goal in the short term — wants to be profitable in year one to justify not taking a high-paying consulting job.
Barbershop only intends to initially sell haircut service. Any other additional products or services can be considered in the future.

interviewer_notes: Problem: develop a market entry strategy for Busch's Barber Shop. Key case steps: (1) develop a structure, (2) confirm market attractiveness/size, (3) calculate revenue and costs for two potential locations, (4) evaluate profitability of a potential loyalty program, (5) brainstorm other areas of consideration, (6) provide client recommendation.

suggested_framework.summary: A sample structure covering client goals, market size/growth/competition, profitability (volume, pricing, costs), go-to-market strategy, barriers, and risks.

tree.label: Should my friend start Busch's Barber Shop?

children.label: Price elasticity, pricing method (e.g. loyalty), service mix
Costs: fixed (rent, equipment, merchandise, advertising) and variable (labor)
Build, acquire, or partner with additional co-owner

stages.interviewer_asks: Develop a framework for how to approach this new venture.
stages.release_when: Only after candidate asks — release the clarifying information (target customer, competitive dynamics, market growth, friend's constraints, product scope) on request.
stages.info_to_release: Clarifying information: male-only target market; two-segment, highly competitive market with a perceived middle-ground opportunity; market growing at GDP; friend has savings but no cosmetology experience and wants year-one profitability; haircuts-only product initially.
stages.expected_answer: A structure covering Client (goals/resources), Market (size, growth, competition, segmentation), Profitability (volume, pricing/service mix, fixed and variable costs), Go-to-market strategy (build/acquire/partner), Barriers (capital, regulation, talent), and Risks (competitive response, differentiation, opportunity cost).
good_answer_signals: Structure is MECE and tailored to a small-business market-entry decision, not just a generic profitability tree
Explicitly separates fixed vs. variable costs
Surfaces the friend's personal constraints (capital, no experience) as a distinct bucket

stages.interviewer_asks: Following discussion of the framework, briefly market-size the adult men's haircut market in Evanston.
stages.expected_answer: There is no single correct answer. A good approach walks through: city population (~60k), male/female ratio (~50/50), % of men who pay for haircuts, % who get cut in Evanston vs. downtown Chicago, average annual haircuts per person, and price segmentation (high-end vs. low-end average prices and the split between them) — ending in a total annual dollar amount spent on haircuts by Evanston men.
good_answer_signals: Makes clearly-labeled, defensible assumptions rather than guessing silently
Moves quickly since this sizing is not the primary purpose of the case
Shows structure and intuition rather than aiming for a single 'right' number

stages.interviewer_asks: Your friend thinks there is a profitable middle ground between the low-cost/low-quality cut and the high-cost/high-quality cut markets. Calculate the revenue and costs for two potential locations to determine the optimal choice.
stages.info_to_release: Exhibits A & B, plus: an average Evanston male pays for 10 haircuts/year; the shop is open 10 hours/day, 360 days/year; customers stay with the same barbershop once they choose (no switching back and forth); the survey underlying the customer-steal projections described the new shop as in-between quality at a $30 price point.
stages.expected_answer: Adult male customers: low-end segment = 60k x 50% x 2/3 ≈ 20k; high-end segment = 60k x 50% x 1/3 ≈ 10k. Customers stolen: Downtown = 20k x 10% + 10k x 5% = 2.5k; Not Downtown = 20k x 5% + 10k x 5% = 1.5k. Revenue (customers x 10 cuts/yr x $30): Downtown = $750k; Not Downtown = $450k. Costs: Downtown = $50k upfront + $48k rent (annualized) + $216k labor = $314k; Not Downtown = $55k upfront + $12k rent (annualized) + $108k labor = $175k. Year-1 profit: Downtown = $436k; Not Downtown = $275k. Downtown has higher projected first-year profit and is the recommended location.
good_answer_signals: Correctly applies the 2/3 low-end / 1/3 high-end population split
Annualizes labor correctly using hours/day x days/year
Compares profit, not just revenue, across the two locations
Optionally raises other location factors (long-term plans, proximity, visibility, layout, capacity for growth, demographic fit) if asked

stages.interviewer_asks: Your friend (having chosen the downtown location) is considering a loyalty program: give customers their 10th haircut free, projected to increase total first-year customers by 10%. Is this a profitable decision?
stages.release_when: After the location decision is made.
stages.info_to_release: Costs are assumed to remain constant (no marginal cost per haircut since employees are hourly and no additional hires are needed).
stages.expected_answer: New customer count = 2,500 x 110% = 2,750. Expected revenue with the loyalty program = 2,750 customers x (10 - 1) paid haircuts x $30 = $742.5k, versus $750k without the program. Since costs don't change, this is a small net revenue decline (~1%) and not a profitable decision as modeled — though the decline is minimal, so it's worth asking whether other benefits (building customer base in year one, upselling additional products/services to the larger base) could still justify it.
good_answer_signals: Correctly subtracts the one free haircut when computing paid haircuts per customer (9, not 10)
Notices costs are assumed flat and states why
Goes beyond the yes/no answer to note the decline is small and could be justified by other strategic benefits

stages.interviewer_asks: (Optional) What changes could be made to make the loyalty program profitable? What are the pros and cons of a membership-based pricing model (a flat monthly fee for unlimited haircuts) instead, and how would you think about setting its price? What are some ways to attract and retain quality talent without paying as much as high-end competitors?
stages.expected_answer: Loyalty fix ideas: decrease the frequency of free cuts, or make the reward 50% off instead of fully free, etc. Membership pros: more predictable revenue, more customer data, differentiation. Membership cons: adverse selection (only heavy users sign up), potentially unhappy employees if tips fall under the new payment scheme. Talent ideas: more flexible schedules, end-of-year profit sharing to build ownership, recruiting rising stars from the low-end market before they move up.
good_answer_signals: Generates multiple distinct ideas per sub-question rather than one
Flags adverse selection as a specific risk of membership pricing
Ties talent strategy back to the shop's cost structure (avoiding high-end base wages)

stages.expected_answer: Your friend should choose the downtown location for starting his new barbershop, without the loyalty program (projected first-year profit ≈$430k+; implementing the free-10th-haircut program decreases revenue under current growth expectations). Risks: the numbers assume immediate customer acquisition, which is unrealistic without an effective marketing campaign; competitive response is possible but the projected steal from the high-end segment is only 5%, unlikely to cause a drastic reaction; customers may not perceive enough of a quality increase to justify a higher price vs. other low-end options; and there are opportunity costs (other uses of capital, other locations, or buying an existing shop instead of starting new). Next steps: due diligence on buying an existing shop; more extensive customer surveys to confirm projections; research hiring qualified barbers; sign lease, purchase equipment, bring on an advisor, and develop a marketing strategy; revisit changes to the loyalty program to improve its profitability.
good_answer_signals: Recommendation is specific (location + no loyalty program) and quantified
Risk list goes beyond generic 'competition' to reference the actual projected steal percentages
Next steps are concrete and sequenced

exhibits.key_insight: Two-thirds of the existing market is low-end (cheap, low quality) and one-third is high-end (overpriced), consistent with the friend's premise that a mid-market gap exists.

exhibits.title: Competitors' market share by segment
exhibits.description: Two stacked bar charts (100% each) showing the market-share split among existing competitors within the low-end segment and within the high-end segment.
exhibits.key_insight: The low-end segment is more fragmented (five competitors) while the high-end segment is more concentrated (three competitors), which is context for how much customer 'steal' a new entrant might realistically capture.

exhibits.title: Market Entry Projections (two candidate locations)
exhibits.description: Table comparing two potential locations (Downtown vs. Not Downtown) on expected customer steal from the low-end and high-end segments, upfront costs (equipment, advertising), and ongoing costs (rent, labor).
exhibits.key_insight: Downtown has a higher expected customer steal and higher rent/advertising, while Not Downtown is cheaper to run but captures fewer customers — the tradeoff the location math resolves.

math.answer: Low-end ≈ 20k adult male customers; High-end ≈ 10k adult male customers.

givens: Downtown steals 10% of low-end (20k) and 5% of high-end (10k) customers

givens: Not Downtown steals 5% of low-end (20k) and 5% of high-end (10k) customers

givens: Labor: 4 workers x $15/hr x 10 hr/day x 360 days/year

math.question: What are total year-1 costs for the Not Downtown location?
givens: Labor: 2 workers x $15/hr x 10 hr/day x 360 days/year

math.answer: Downtown location wins with ≈$436k year-1 profit vs. $275k for Not Downtown.

math.question: Is the proposed loyalty program (free 10th haircut, +10% total customers) a profitable decision for the Downtown location?
givens: Under the program, customers pay for only 9 of every 10 haircuts
Costs assumed constant (no marginal cost per cut)
math.answer: Revenue falls by ≈$7.5k (from $750k to $742.5k); since costs are unchanged, this is not a profitable decision as modeled, though the decline is small (~1%).

synthesis: Your friend should choose the downtown location for starting his new barbershop, without the loyalty program — projected first-year profits of ~$430k. Implementing the free-10th-haircut loyalty program results in decreased revenue at current growth expectations. Key risks: the numbers assume immediate customer acquisition, which is unrealistic without an effective marketing campaign; possible competitive response from high-end stores, though unlikely to be drastic given only 5% projected steal from that segment; customers may not perceive enough quality increase to justify the price versus other low-end options; and there are opportunity costs (other uses of capital, other possible locations, or buying an existing shop instead of starting new).
what_great_looks_like: Builds a tailored, MECE framework rather than reciting a generic profitability tree
Moves quickly and confidently through the market-sizing exercise, since it is a secondary check rather than the core of the case
Compares profit (not just revenue) across the two locations and correctly annualizes monthly rent and hourly labor
Catches the '9 paid haircuts, not 10' nuance in the loyalty-program math
Surfaces real business risks and concrete next steps in the final recommendation, not just a location choice
common_pitfalls: Spending too long on the market-sizing exercise instead of moving quickly as instructed
Forgetting to annualize the monthly rent figure before comparing it to annual revenue
Counting 10 paid haircuts instead of 9 in the loyalty-program revenue calculation
Recommending purely on revenue rather than profit when comparing the two locations
Treating the loyalty program's small revenue decline as automatically disqualifying without considering strategic upside
follow_ups: What other factors should be considered when choosing a potential shop location (long-term plans, proximity, transportation, visibility, layout, capacity for growth, demographic preference)?
What changes could make the loyalty program profitable?
What are the pros/cons of membership-based pricing, and how would you set its price?
How would you attract and retain quality talent without paying high-end wages?
